questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why industrialization began in Britain?
choices: Britain's ban on trade with other countries
Coal and iron alone, without any role for labor, capital, or overseas trade
Coal and iron, available labor, capital, and access to markets
Britain's lack of overseas colonies
questions.explanation: Historians cite several factors working together.
choiceExplanations: Britain traded widely.
Resources alone do not explain it.
Historians cite several factors working together.
Britain had extensive colonies.
questions.distinguisher: Coal and iron mattered, but historians combine them with labor, capital, and markets.

questions.prompt: The factory system is best described as
choices: workers using machines in a central workplace on fixed hours
families spinning thread at home for merchants
guilds controlling production in towns
workers using machines in their own homes and on their own schedules
questions.explanation: Factories gathered workers and machines under one roof on fixed schedules.
choiceExplanations: Factories gathered workers and machines under one roof on fixed schedules.
Home spinning was the putting-out system.
Guilds belong to earlier town economies.
Factories replaced home production and fixed the hours.
questions.distinguisher: Work at home on one's own schedule describes the older putting-out system, not factories.

questions.prompt: Steam engines changed the location of factories because they
choices: required factories to be built in rural mountain valleys
were powered by wind instead of water
freed mills from the need for any fuel
freed mills from the need to be built beside fast rivers
questions.explanation: Steam power let mills move to cities near coal and workers.
choiceExplanations: Steam let mills move to cities.
Steam engines burned coal.
Steam engines needed coal.
Steam power let mills move to cities near coal and workers.
questions.distinguisher: Steam freed mills from rivers, but it needed coal as fuel.

questions.prompt: The enclosure movement contributed to industrialization by
choices: pushing rural laborers to emigrate to India to work on British plantations
pushing rural laborers toward towns where factories needed workers
giving peasants more common land to farm
ending agriculture in Britain
questions.explanation: Enclosure raised output and displaced laborers who moved to towns.
choiceExplanations: Displaced laborers mostly moved to British towns.
Enclosure raised output and displaced laborers who moved to towns.
Enclosure removed common land.
Farming continued and became more productive.
questions.distinguisher: Enclosure pushed laborers to towns, not to India.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would most directly support the argument that overseas trade contributed to British industrialization?
choices: Evidence that British mills used water power
Evidence that raw cotton from the Americas supplied British mills
Evidence that Britain had large coal deposits
Evidence that British farms became more productive
questions.explanation: Imported raw cotton shows overseas trade feeding industry.
choiceExplanations: Water power is domestic.
Imported raw cotton shows overseas trade feeding industry.
Coal is domestic.
Farm productivity is domestic.
questions.distinguisher: Coal was important, but it is a domestic resource, not evidence about overseas trade.

questions.prompt: The author's main argument is that industrialization began in Britain because of
choices: overseas trade alone
several factors working together
the discovery of coal alone
government ownership of factories
questions.explanation: The author lists coal, farming change, capital, government, and trade.
choiceExplanations: Trade is one factor.
The author lists coal, farming change, capital, government, and trade.
Coal is one factor among several.
The passage does not mention state factories.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.3 key concept: a variety of factors led to the rise of industrial production, including Europe's location on the Atlantic, geographic distribution of coal, iron, and timber, urbanization, and access to foreign resources
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing why industrialization began in Britain, c. 1750–1830
stimulusBlocks.text:
Historians point to several reasons that industrial production began in Britain. Britain had large deposits of coal and iron ore near rivers and ports. Improvements in farming, along with the enclosure of common lands, raised food output and pushed laborers toward towns. Merchants and landowners had capital to invest, and banks and a stable government protected property.

Overseas trade mattered too. Colonies and the Atlantic trade supplied raw cotton and markets for finished cloth. Some historians stress that cheap coal and high wages made it profitable for British manufacturers to replace workers with machines.

questions.prompt: The historians mentioned in the final sentence would most likely agree that
choices: machines replaced coal as a fuel
machines were adopted where they saved money
machines were adopted because labor was cheap
machines were invented only in Britain
questions.explanation: Cheap coal and high wages made machines profitable.
choiceExplanations: Machines used coal.
Cheap coal and high wages made machines profitable.
They say wages were high.
The historians discuss why machines paid off in Britain, not where they were invented.
questions.distinguisher: They stress high wages, not cheap labor, as the reason machines paid off.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, Arkwright's mills changed work by
choices: gathering workers under one roof on fixed hours
letting workers spin thread at home for merchants
ending the use of water power in spinning mills
paying workers by the piece at home
questions.explanation: His mills gathered hundreds of workers on fixed hours.
choiceExplanations: His mills gathered hundreds of workers on fixed hours.
Mills replaced home spinning.
The water frame used water power.
That is the putting-out system.
questions.distinguisher: Piecework at home describes the older putting-out system.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.3 key concept: the development of machines, including steam engines, and the factory system transformed production, beginning with textiles
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the mechanization of British cotton manufacturing, 1760–1830
stimulusBlocks.text:
Cotton spinning was transformed first. The spinning jenny of the 1760s let one worker spin many threads at once, and Richard Arkwright's water frame, patented in 1769, used water power to spin strong thread. Arkwright built mills that gathered hundreds of workers under one roof, keeping them on fixed hours.

When steam engines replaced water wheels, mills no longer had to be built beside fast rivers and could be placed in cities near coal and workers. Manchester grew from a market town into the center of a world cotton industry.

move closer to fast rivers
move into cities near coal and workers
stop using cotton from the Americas
questions.explanation: Steam power let mills be built in cities such as Manchester.
choiceExplanations: Production became more centralized.
Steam removed the need for rivers.
Steam power let mills be built in cities such as Manchester.
Mills still used cotton.

questions.prompt: Which feature of production does Smith describe in the passage?
choices: Each worker makes an entire pin from start to finish
Machines replace human workers in making pins
Pin-makers work alone in their homes for merchants
Making a pin is divided into specialized steps carried out by different workers
questions.explanation: Smith lists the separate steps, such as drawing the wire, cutting it, and putting on the head, performed by different people.
choiceExplanations: He describes the opposite: workers who each do one or two operations.
The passage describes workers, not machines.
He describes a workshop, not home production.
Smith lists the separate steps, such as drawing the wire, cutting it, and putting on the head, performed by different people.
questions.distinguisher: Some workers did two or three operations, but the point is the division into distinct tasks.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Adam Smith, Scottish philosopher and economist, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, 1776
stimulusBlocks.citation: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, ch. 1. Project Gutenberg eBook #3300.
stimulusBlocks.note: A manufactory is a workshop. Smith is describing the division of labor in pin-making.
stimulusBlocks.text: One man draws out the wire; another straights it; a third cuts it; a fourth points it; a fifth grinds it at the top for receiving the head; to make the head requires two or three distinct operations; to put it on is a peculiar business; to whiten the pins is another; it is even a trade by itself to put them into the paper; and the important business of making a pin is, in this manner, divided into about eighteen distinct operations, which, in some manufactories, are all performed by distinct hands, though in others the same man will sometimes perform two or three of them. I have seen a small manufactory of this kind, where ten men only were employed, and where some of them consequently performed two or three distinct operations.

questions.prompt: The division of labor Smith describes most directly contributed to
choices: a return to artisan craft production in small shops
higher output per worker in factory production
the decline of manufacturing in Britain and Europe
the end of wage labor throughout industry
questions.explanation: Specialized tasks allowed workers to produce far more than if each made a whole product.
choiceExplanations: Division of labor moved production away from the craft model.
Specialized tasks allowed workers to produce far more than if each made a whole product.
It supported the growth of manufacturing.
Division of labor increased wage labor in factories.
questions.distinguisher: Craftwork continued, but the division of labor changed how many goods were made.

questions.prompt: How would Marx and Engels in 1848 most likely have interpreted the kind of work Smith describes?
choices: As work that makes people “an appendage of the machine”
As a model for farm work organized under feudal lords
As proof that workers had become wealthier than capitalists
As an example of artisans controlling their own tools
questions.explanation: Marx and Engels wrote that division of labor had stripped workers' tasks of individual character.
choiceExplanations: Marx and Engels wrote that division of labor had stripped workers' tasks of individual character.
Marx and Engels were describing industrial work, not feudal farming.
They argued that workers were exploited, not wealthier.
They described workers losing control over their tools.
questions.distinguisher: Smith saw division of labor as a source of prosperity, while Marx and Engels emphasized its human costs.
